parts:
Thanks.

We strongly recommend not including Stan programs in R
programs as strings because you lose line numbers in messages, and
you either lose transpose (') or quotes for print ("). I'd also
recommend following our layout style (follows Google C++ style),
but that's up to you; the non-standard layouts are harder for us
to follow and they almost all use too much vertical space for
the number of lines of code.

Also, you probably meant "book" instead of "bppk" in the comment.

We'd also suggest putting priors directly on scale (sigma)
rather than squared scale (your sigma2). See the manual chapter
on regression for recommendations.

You can make mu a local variable inside the model, or even replace
mu with B * theta in the normal sampling statement, which will cut
down on the output.

We're happy to accept working case studies with some text explanation
of what's going on. I particularly like replications of work that's
appeared elsewhere, becuase we can check we're getting the right answer.

- Bob

Dear Lawrence

The number and place of knots is solved by using Penalty in B-Spline. When we use Penalty in B-Spline, we can choose a large number of knots (about 10 to 20 is recommended) to ensure the desired flexibility. In fact, the penalty control the variance of estimated parameters. If change "num_knots= 20" in attached file (for instance 15 , 30), you will see the results do not change much.

Comparing GPR and Penalized B-Spline is a good idea. I will do it as soon as possible and inform you. If you have the Stan model of GPR, please send me it.

- Bistoon

You probably want to scale your inputs if using those priors, so do

    x = scale(range)[,1]
    y = scale(logratio)[,1]
    xnew = x

Then after sampling remember to rescale back:
    yhat_gpr = rep(NA,length(xnew))
    for(i in 1:length(xnew)) 
  yhat_gpr[i] = M[paste0('y2[',i,']'),'mean']*sd(logratio)+mean(logratio)
    plot(range,logratio)
    lines(range, yhat_gpr, col="#ED7D31", lwd=3)

parts:
And it's useful to see the intervals for the predictions:

library(tidyverse)
y2 = rstan::extract(fit,pars='y2')[[1]]
y2 = y2 * sd(logratio) + mean(logratio)
data.frame(y2) %>%
tidyr::gather('x','value') %>%
dplyr::group_by(x) %>%
dplyr::summarise(
lo95 = quantile(value,.025)
, hi95 = quantile(value,.975)
, sig = (lo95>0)|(hi95<0)
, lo50 = quantile(value,.25)
, hi50 = quantile(value,.75)
, med = quantile(value,.5)
) %>%
dplyr::mutate(
x_num = as.numeric(gsub('X','',x))
, range = range[x_num]
) %>%
ggplot2::ggplot(
mapping = aes(
x = range
, y = med
)
)+
ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
mapping = aes(
ymin = lo95
, ymax = hi95
)
, alpha = .5
)+
ggplot2::geom_ribbon(
mapping = aes(
ymin = lo50
, ymax = hi50
)
, alpha = .5
)+
ggplot2::geom_line()+
ggplot2::geom_point(
data = data.frame(
range = range
, logratio = logratio
)
, mapping = aes(
x = range
, y = logratio
)
, alpha = .5
)

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian Penalized B-Spline Code (rstan)
parts: At the bottom of the wiki entry on prior choice recommendations (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations) is a section for Gaussian Processes. The first bullet describes the student_t(4,0,1) prior for inv_rho (called "rho" in the code Bistoon linked because I was being a lazy typist). The second bullet refers to the eta & sigma parameters, and that setting the same prior for each is akin to setting a prior on the signal-to-noise as peaked at .5, but that bullet refers to a 0 peaked normal(0,1), which I've subsequently been replacing with weibul(2,1), which is peaked at a little less than 1 and goes to zero at 0.

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

parts:
Dear Seth,

execellent. I'll try out your idea. 
Meanwhile I have had a look at
the c++ implementation of cov_exp_quad. It's in file:
stan/math/prim/mat/fun/cov_exp_quad.hpp
of stan math library.

The implementation of 
          cov(i, j) = sigma_sq * exp(squared_distance(x[i], x[j])
                                     * neg_half_inv_l_sq);

could be speed up:
     log_sigma_sq = log(sigma_sq);
     //...    
     cov(i, j) = exp(log_sigma_sq + squared_distance(x[i], x[j])
                                     * neg_half_inv_l_sq);

sigma_sq >= 0 
and since squared_distance in many cases is constant it could be moved out. 

      T_sigma sigma_sq = square(sigma);
      T_l neg_half_inv_l_sq = - 0.5 / square(l);


      for (int j = 0; j < (x_size - 1); ++j) {
        cov(j, j) = sigma_sq;
        for (int i = j + 1; i < x_size; ++i) {
          cov(i, j) = sigma_sq * exp(squared_distance(x[i], x[j])
                                     * neg_half_inv_l_sq);
          cov(j, i) = cov(i, j);
        }
      }
      cov(x_size - 1, x_size - 1) = sigma_sq;
      return cov;

Andre

That'd cost a log plus x_size adds vs. x_size multiplies. For
any reasonably x_size, it's probably a win. At higher order, it's
also a simpler chain rule.

Daniel and I had a brief discussion off list. Daniel writes:

> With a 1000 obs of 10 vectors, it takes ~5 seconds to do the computation 1000 times. If you
> think we have 10 leapfrog steps on average, it'll be ~50 seconds. It's still not a killer, but maybe
> it's worth it.

And my response:

That's right, and I think we're hoping eventually to be able to
routinely do 5000-10000 observations based on other speedups!

I recognize it's annoying to maintain the codebase, but from a user's
point of view it seems pretty natural for there to be this option. I
just went to see what the R package RandomFields does and the function
RFcovmatrix which creates a covariance matrix for a specified kernel
takes either x or x1 and x2 (so far just like Stan) or the lower
triangular part of a matrix of a matrix of distances. There's no lower
triangular data type, so I'd propose the following design:

data {
int n;
int p;
vector[n] x[p];
}

transformed data {
matrix[n,n] D;

for(i in 1:n)
for(j in 1:n)

D[i,j] = distance(x[i], x[j]);
}
parameters {
real lengthscale;
}

transformed parameters {
cov_matrix[n] K;
K = cov_exp_quad(D, 1, lengthscale);
}

Which would be a more efficient version of:

K = cov_exp_quad(x, 1, lengthscale);

Does that make sense?

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian Penalized B-Spline Code (rstan)
parts:
Thanks, Bob.

I was trying to mention that there's a design issue with cov_exp_quad() and accepting matrix as the first argument. There isn't one natural way to treat a matrix. This was the second time this week that someone's asked that cov_exp_quad() accept a matrix as the first argument, but it wasn't to accept the distance matrix. Here are 3 sensible ways users might expect a cov_exp_quad() function to work accepting a matrix as the first argument:
1. treat the matrix as a distance matrix (what Seth is thinking). This might save some computation.
2. treat the columns of the matrix as observations (what Aki is thinking). This would be identical to an array of vectors as the first argument. This might save some user confusion and indexing issues.
3. treat the rows of the matrix as observations (what Ben thinks is natural and anyone that uses something like R). This would be identical to providing an array of row_vectors as the first argument. This also saves some user confusion and indexing issues.

The design issue is this: which one of these do we implement?

Once we introduce one of these implementations to our users, that's it. That's what the function means. That's why I had suggested that if you're really keen on implementing this function, that it be called something different, like cov_exp_quad_with_distance_matrix().

That said, if someone were to implement option 1 fully, there's a good chance we would just accept it as the default behavior. Actions speak much louder than words. (or option 2 or 3.)


Hope that makes sense.


Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Bayesian Penalized B-Spline Code (rstan)
parts:
> On Oct 26, 2016, at 2:41 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>
> Thanks, Bob.
>
> I was trying to mention that there's a design issue with cov_exp_quad() and accepting matrix as the first argument. There isn't one natural way to treat a matrix. This was the second time this week that someone's asked that cov_exp_quad() accept a matrix as the first argument, but it wasn't to accept the distance matrix. Here are 3 sensible ways users might expect a cov_exp_quad() function to work accepting a matrix as the first argument:
> 1. treat the matrix as a distance matrix (what Seth is thinking). This might save some computation.
> 2. treat the columns of the matrix as observations (what Aki is thinking). This would be identical to an array of vectors as the first argument. This might save some user confusion and indexing issues.
> 3. treat the rows of the matrix as observations (what Ben thinks is natural and anyone that uses something like R). This would be identical to providing an array of row_vectors as the first argument. This also saves some user confusion and indexing issues.

(3) is also the usual stats notation, which is why you can
write X * beta in regressions. It also follows all of our
example code. I don't think we want to do (2) because it
doesn't match our other conventions (you'd get beta' * X
in regressions).

Is it restricted to univariate now instead of multivariate
observations? That seems very limiting, so I'd be inclined
to go with (3). But then if you go with (1), the distance can get
computed on the outside, which is a plus for flexibility but
also defeats some of the purpose of having a built-in function.

We could then build two distance-matrix building functions, one
for univariate input, one for multivariate output, and then Aki
can just transpose for (2). This would be good especially if what
we want to do is encourage people to use the more efficient form (1).

Longer names vs. overloading is a separate issue to which if any
of these we'll implement.

The higher level the function, the harder it is to specify a clean
interface that covers all the usages.

- Bob

Refering to end of 15.2 in manual

L = cholesky_decompose(Sigma);
y = mu + L * z;

where  Sigma = eta * exp( ... );

we could also write L = sqrt(eta) * cholesky_decompose(exp(...)));

Thus if we write y = mu + sqrt(eta) * (cholesky_decompose(exp(...)) * z);
Then we change the complexity of the multiplication with eta
from O(n^2) to O(n), requiring the move from multi_normal to normal. 

We would only need then a fast function which does

exp(X) of a triangular matrix.
